summary: An FAQ-style article introducing Reiki and Qigong as energy healing practices rooted in Asian traditions. It explains what each involves, who may benefit, the research (mixed, with some studies suggesting effects beyond placebo), typical costs and insurance, how to find a practitioner, and possible side effects. It stresses consulting a healthcare provider and treating these as complementary to conventional medicine.
one_line: FAQ guide to Reiki and Qigong covering how they work, benefits, research evidence, costs, finding practitioners, and safety.
key_facts: Energy healing rests on the idea that a subtle life force, called 'qi' in Chinese medicine and 'ki' in Japanese tradition, flows through the body and can be balanced to assist healing.
Reiki originated in Japan in the early 20th century and was founded by Mikao Usui on September 15, 1922.
In Reiki, a practitioner channels energy through touch, placing hands lightly on or just above the clothed body in specific hand positions.
Reiki sessions usually last between 45 minutes to an hour and a half and need no special equipment.
Qigong (pronounced 'chee-gung') is a centuries-old Chinese health care system combining physical postures, breathing techniques, and focused intention; it has been practiced for over 4,000 years.
'Qi' means life force or vital energy, while 'Gong' denotes the skill of cultivating self-discipline and achievement.
Qigong sessions can range from a few minutes to an hour and are often practiced alone, though also in groups or with a teacher.
Both practices are considered non-invasive and safe, and may help with stress and anxiety, chronic pain, fatigue, and emotional unrest.
A randomized study published October 14, 2023 in the 'Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine' found Reiki reduced anxiety and improved mood compared with those who did not receive it.
A study released September 3, 2023 found Qigong improved blood pressure and stress levels in participants after three months of practice.
A systematic review dated September 12, 2023 indicated Reiki could be more effective than placebo at inducing relaxation.
A Reiki session typically costs $50 to over $100, while group Qigong classes cost about $10 to $30 per session.
Some insurers in certain regions may cover Reiki or Qigong as part of an integrative health program, particularly when prescribed by a physician.
Possible reactions include emotional release, tingling or warmth, or temporary exacerbation of symptoms (a healing crisis); these are typically short-lived.
The article advises consulting a healthcare provider before starting these practices, and checking practitioner certification and asking for referrals.
